title: PAL: Probing Audio Encoders via LLMs -- A Study of Information Transfer from Audio Encoders to LLMs
summary:
The integration of audio perception capabilities into Large Language Models
(LLMs) has enabled significant advances in Audio-LLMs. Although
application-focused developments, particularly in curating training data for
specific capabilities e.g., audio reasoning, have progressed rapidly, the
underlying mechanisms that govern efficient transfer of rich semantic
representations from audio encoders to LLMs remain under-explored. We
conceptualize effective audio-LLM interaction as the LLM's ability to
proficiently probe the audio encoder representations to satisfy textual
queries. This paper presents a systematic investigation on how architectural
design choices can affect that. Beginning with a standard Pengi/LLaVA-style
audio-LLM architecture, we propose and evaluate several modifications guided by
hypotheses derived from mechanistic interpretability studies and LLM
operational principles. Our experiments demonstrate that: (1) delaying audio
integration until the LLM's initial layers establish textual context that
enhances its ability to probe the audio representations for relevant
information; (2) the LLM can proficiently probe audio representations
exclusively through LLM layer's attention submodule, without requiring
propagation to its Feed-Forward Network (FFN) submodule; (3) an efficiently
integrated ensemble of diverse audio encoders provides richer, complementary
representations, thereby broadening the LLM's capacity to probe a wider
spectrum of audio information. All hypotheses are evaluated using an identical
three-stage training curriculum on a dataset of 5.6 million audio-text pairs,
ensuring controlled comparisons. Our final architecture, which incorporates all
proposed modifications, achieves relative improvements from 10\% to 60\% over
the baseline, validating our approach to optimizing cross-modal information
transfer in audio-LLMs. Project page: https://ta012.github.io/PAL/

bib.abstract: Each edition of the challenge on Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events (DCASE) contained several tasks involving sound event detection in different setups. DCASE 2017 presented participants with three such tasks, each having specific datasets and detection requirements: Task 2, in which target sound events were very rare in both training and testing data, Task 3 having overlapping events annotated in real-life audio, and Task 4, in which only weakly-labeled data was available for training. In this paper, we present the three tasks, including the datasets and baseline systems, and analyze the challenge entries for each task. We observe the popularity of methods using deep neural networks, and the still widely used mel frequency based representations, with only few approaches standing out as radically different. Analysis of the systems behavior reveals that task-specific optimization has a big role in producing good performance; however, often this optimization closely follows the ranking metric, and its maximization/minimization does not result in universally good performance. We also introduce the calculation of confidence intervals based on a jackknife resampling procedure, to perform statistical analysis of the challenge results. The analysis indicates that while the 95\% confidence intervals for many systems overlap, there are significant difference in performance between the top systems and the baseline for all tasks.
bib.title: Sound event detection in the {DCASE} 2017 Challenge

\begin{abstract}
The integration of audio perception capabilities into Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled significant advances in Audio-LLMs. Although application-focused developments, particularly in curating training data for specific capabilities e.g., audio reasoning, have progressed rapidly, the underlying mechanisms that govern efficient transfer of rich semantic representations from audio encoders to LLMs remain under-explored. We conceptualize effective audio-LLM interaction as the LLM's ability to proficiently probe the audio encoder representations to satisfy textual queries. This paper presents a systematic investigation on how architectural design choices can affect that. Beginning with a standard Pengi/LLaVA-style audio-LLM architecture, we propose and evaluate several modifications guided by hypotheses derived from mechanistic interpretability studies and LLM operational principles. Our experiments demonstrate that: (1) delaying audio integration until the LLM's initial layers establish textual context that enhances its ability to probe the audio representations for relevant information; (2) the LLM can proficiently probe audio representations exclusively through LLM layer's attention submodule, without requiring propagation to its Feed-Forward Network (FFN) submodule; (3) an efficiently integrated ensemble of diverse audio encoders provides richer, complementary representations, thereby broadening the LLM's capacity to probe a wider spectrum of audio information. All hypotheses are evaluated using an identical three-stage training curriculum on a dataset of 5.6 million audio-text pairs, ensuring controlled comparisons. Our final architecture, which incorporates all proposed modifications, achieves relative improvements from 10\% to 60\% over the baseline, validating our approach to optimizing cross-modal information transfer in audio-LLMs. Project page: \url{https://ta012.github.io/PAL/}
\end{abstract}



\section{Introduction}

Large Language Models (LLMs)~\cite{brown2020language,grattafiori2024llama,jiang2024mixtral,liu2024deepseek} have emerged as the foundational technology for natural language interaction with machines, demonstrating remarkable conversational fluency. Despite this success, their perceptual capabilities remain limited primarily to text, restricting their ability to understand the physical world. This limitation has inspired significant research into multi-modal LLMs (MLLMs)~\cite{liu2023visual,gong2024listen,zhu2023minigpt,jiang2024mixtral,maaz2023video}, which expand traditional LLMs by integrating additional sensory modalities such as vision (Vision LLMs)~\cite{liu2023visual,templeton2024scaling,wang2024cogvlm}, audio (Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) or simply audio-LLMs)~\cite{deshmukh2023pengi,gong2024listen,tang2024salmonn,ghosh2024gama,ghosh2025audio}, and other inputs~\cite{brohan2023rt,thawkar2023xraygpt} to foster more natural, intuitive, and effective human-machine interfaces.

%%% About LALMs
%Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) also referred to as 
Audio-LLMs, aim to integrate audio representations generated by various audio encoders into LLMs. A widely adopted architectural approach is the Pengi/LLaVA~\cite{deshmukh2023pengi,liu2023visual} style, exemplified by audio-LLMs such as Pengi~\cite{deshmukh2023pengi}, LTU~\cite{gong2024listen}, SALMONN~\cite{tang2024salmonn} and GAMA~\cite{ghosh2024gama}. 
These architectures project audio embeddings into the LLMs' input word embedding space. 
%These architectures project audio embeddings into a unified embedding space aligned with the tokenizer outputs of LLMs. 
The resulting audio embeddings are prepended to textual tokens, enabling the LLM to process audio alongside text, effectively treating audio information as additional textual tokens. An alternative architectural approach inspired by Flamingo~\cite{alayrac2022flamingo} is the Audio-Flamingo architecture~\cite{kong2024audio}. Audio-Flamingo introduces cross-attention and Feed-Forward Network (FFN) blocks inserted between successive LLM layers to pass audio representations via latent token into the LLM\@. Within the new cross-attention block, textual tokens attend to latent audio tokens, then are passed to cross-attention block's FFN module, before proceeding to the LLM's next layer. 
% \( l \). % cross-attend to audio tokens before proceeding to layer \( l+1 \).

%The empirical effectiveness of these architectural choices remains an open question. Each work employs its own training data, pre-training curricula, making direct comparisons difficult. Currently, there is no standard benchmark or study that rigorously compares these approaches in a unified experimental setting.

%% Motivation
Recent advances in audio representation learning have yielded powerful models through self-supervised methods like Audio-MAE~\cite{huang2022amae}, BEATs~\cite{chen2022beats}, ASiT~\cite{Ahmed_2024}, EAT~\cite{chen2024eat}, SSLAM~\cite{alex2025sslam} and multi-modal supervised approaches such as CLAP~\cite{elizalde2023clap} , LAION-CLAP~\cite{wu2023large}, ReCLAP~\cite{ghosh2025reclap}. While these models learn rich audio representations, they typically reside in abstract embedding spaces, necessitating further engineering for downstream tasks like audio event detection or acoustic scene analysis. A common technique, \textit{linear probing}, involves training a simple linear layer on these representations for specific tasks; yet the outputs from such probing are not inherently human-interpretable. We posit that audio-LLMs provide a more direct interface, allowing \textit{humans to probe these sophisticated audio representations} through natural language interaction.
Consequently, to enable an LLM to effectively probe audio encoder representations and satisfy textual queries, the connection mechanism must effectively transfer crucial audio details, such as event signals and temporal dynamics, from the audio encoder into the LLM's embedding and concept space. Once the LLM receives this information, it can leverage its reasoning and generative capabilities to respond appropriately to user queries, whether requiring concise answers, detailed explanations, or the generation of more complex and contextually nuanced textual outputs, such as poetry adhering to specific rhyming schemes. Therefore, ensuring this signal effectively reaches the LLM's conceptual space is fundamental. Our exploration specifically focuses on optimizing this information transfer. Furthermore, recent advances in mechanistic interpretability~\cite{bricken2023monosemanticity,templeton2024scaling}, particularly techniques like sparse autoencoders~\cite{bricken2023monosemanticity}, offer valuable tools for understanding the internal workings of LLMs. We use these insights from interpretability studies to guide architectural design choices for improved information flow.

%% Contributions
In this paper, we conduct a principled comparative study focused on the information transfer mechanisms from audio encoders to LLMs. Beginning with a baseline architecture inspired by the Pengi or LLaVA style (e.g., Pengi, LTU, GAMA), we systematically investigate architectural modifications. Each modification is motivated by a specific hypothesis regarding information flow. We evaluate these modifications through detailed empirical analysis, employing a standardized training curriculum and dataset to ensure fair comparisons. Our objective is to identify architectural designs that facilitate efficient information transfer from the audio encoder to the LLM, balancing performance gains with computational efficiency and minimizing parameter overhead.

Our primary contributions in this work are:

\textbf{1. Novel audio-LLM integration insights:} We propose and systematically investigate various techniques for effective integration of audio modalities with LLMs. Our methodology is intuitive, drawing significant inspiration from mechanistic interpretability research alongside other relevant fields. The key findings of our investigations include: 
\textit{\textbf{Delayed fusion benefits:}} Delaying the introduction of audio representations to later LLM layers (termed ~\textit{delayed fusion}) is more effective, as it enables the LLM to first establish and refine textual context before querying audio information. %allowing initial text-only processing, improves performance by enabling the LLM to first establish a textual context before querying audio information. 
\textit{\textbf{Attention sufficiency:}} Processing audio information exclusively through the LLM's attention mechanism, and subsequently discarding the audio representations before FFN submodules, is a sufficient strategy for effective and efficient audio-language integration, maintaining or improving performance compared to full propagation. \textit{\textbf{Audio encoder ensemble advantage:}} Employing an ensemble of diverse audio encoders, combining a self-supervised encoder for fine-grained semantics with specialized language-aligned encoders for general audio, music, and speech, enhances the audio-LLM's ability to handle varied auditory inputs.

\textbf{2. Fair and rigorous architectural comparisons:} To accurately assess the inherent potential of each audio-LLM architecture, we employ a standardized three-stage training curriculum as in Figure~\ref{figStages}, ensuring consistency across critical factors like pre-training data, batch size, training epochs, and overall curriculum design.

\textbf{3. Development of a novel audio-LLM:} Based on the insights gained, we have developed a new audio-LLM architecture that incorporates these findings.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: First, we present our architectural hypotheses and their corresponding empirical evaluations. Next, we detail our experimental setup, including the standardized training curriculum and datasets used to ensure fair comparisons. We then discuss our model's performance relative to prior art. The Appendix contains supplementary qualitative assessments, featuring both human evaluations and AI-based comparisons of output samples between our approach and previous works.

\section{Methodology: Investigating architectural design hypotheses}
\label{arch_analysis}


This section begins by defining a baseline audio-LLM architecture. Next, we introduce and empirically evaluate the proposed architectural improvements using the three-stage training curriculum detailed in Figure~\ref{figStages}(right) and Section~\ref{exp_setup}, guided by specific hypotheses about information flow in the network.

\subsection{Baseline Architecture} %% Exp 1 (ALLM1Feb25)
\label{sec_baseline_arch}
Our baseline audio-LLM adopts the Pengi/LLaVA style architecture for integrating audio, similar to recent works such as Pengi~\cite{deshmukh2023pengi}, LTU~\cite{gong2024listen}, GAMA~\cite{ghosh2024gama} etc. We utilize the self-supervised audio encoder, SSLAM~\cite{alex2025sslam}, to generate audio representations. These representations are then processed through a cross-attention mechanism with learnable latent tokens, followed by a projection layer to map them into the LLM's token embedding space. Further details regarding this latent cross-attention mechanism-based connector module is provided in Section~\ref{sec_hyp3_multi}. The model input follows the sequence: system prompt, audio tokens, user prompt, response. This format is used throughout the paper. We trained this baseline architecture using the experimental setup detailed previously. Evaluation results are presented in Table~\ref{tab_variant_comparision}.

\subsection{Hypothesis 1: Bypassing initial layers for audio integration} %% Exp 2 (AllmL4Fus)
\label{sec_hyp1_delay}
%% This is ireresptive of whether audio tokens have high attenoin scores in early layrs or not
The baseline architecture, as described in Section~\ref{sec_baseline_arch}, integrates audio representations by inserting them between the system prompt and the user prompt tokens in the LLM's input embedding space. We challenge this early integration strategy. Recent mechanistic interpretability studies~\cite{nanda2023factfinding} suggest that the notion of \textit{single-step detokenization} is inaccurate; instead, tokens are gradually converted into meaningful concepts over several initial LLM layers. We hypothesize that inserting audio representations before the LLM has sufficiently processed the textual prompts (system and user) to form initial concepts might hinder its ability to effectively query the audio information. The presence of audio tokens in the very first layers could potentially disrupt the text-based concept formation required to understand the user's query itself.

Based on this reasoning, we propose a \textit{delayed fusion} approach. We hypothesize that delaying the introduction of audio representations until after the initial text-only processing layers will allow the LLM to first establish a textual context, enabling it to better utilize the subsequent audio information. For this experiment, we modify the baseline by bypassing the first four layers for audio integration. The audio representations are introduced starting from the fifth layer of the LLM, as illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig_hyp1_2_3} (A) with $k$\,=\,5, allowing the initial layers to operate solely on the textual tokens.

We evaluated this hypothesis training curriculum, discussed in Section~\ref{training_curriculum}. The results, presented in Table~\ref{tab_variant_comparision}, show improved performance across all training stages compared to the baseline.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=gray!10!white, colframe=gray!75!black, title=\textbf{Finding 1}]
Introducing audio representations after initial text-only processing layers allows the LLM to establish a textual context first. This leads to more effective querying for relevant audio information from the audio representations by the LLM and results in improved overall performance compared to early integration.

\end{tcolorbox}
%%%%%%%%%%%%



\subsection{Hypothesis 2: Attention necessary and sufficient for audio encoder information transfer to LLM} %% Exp 3 V2 (AllmAttnOnlyVisSamMMProjLGapWithAudQ)
% \subsection{Hypothesis 2: Attention is both a Necessary and Sufficient Condition for Audio Encoder Information Transfer to LLM} %% Exp 3 V2 (AllmAttnOnlyVisSamMMProjLGapWithAudQ)
\label{sec_hyp2_attn}

Recent mechanistic interpretability studies of Large Language Models (LLMs) investigate how concepts are represented. LLMs often exhibit superposition, compressing numerous features within hidden activations~\cite{elhage2022superposition}. Sparse autoencoders~\cite{bricken2023monosemanticity,templeton2024scaling} are employed to decompose these, revealing that semantic concepts can correspond to specific, activatable features. For instance, a concept like \textit{"dog"} may be identified with a distinct feature. Activating such a feature, identified via sparse autoencoders, can directly influence model behavior, as demonstrated in the \textit{Golden Gate Bridge Claude}~\cite{templeton2024scaling} experiment, where this caused the LLM to persistently reference the landmark even when un-related questions were asked.

Building on this understanding of concept representation through feature activation, we hypothesize that effective cross-modal grounding in audio-LLMs, specifically for audio-to-LLM concept association, similarly requires audio tokens to induce the activation of relevant sound-related conceptual features within the LLM's textual token embeddings. This mechanism, where distinct auditory inputs trigger corresponding linguistic concept activations, is posited as crucial for an audio-LLM to perform tasks such as answering, \textit{Which animal sound is heard in the audio?} For example, if the input audio contains a~\textit{dog's bark}, we propose that features within the textual embeddings corresponding to the concept \textit{dog} must be activated for the model to correctly associate the auditory stimulus with its linguistic counterpart, mirroring the kind of concept-specific activations observed in text-only LLMs~\cite{bricken2023monosemanticity}.


A standard LLM layer comprises an attention submodule and an FFN submodule. In typical audio-LLM architectures (e.g., Pengi~\cite{deshmukh2023pengi}, LTU~\cite{gong2024listen}, GAMA~\cite{ghosh2024gama}) and the previous variants discussed above, both audio and text tokens are processed through attention and FFN submodules. It is evident from prior studies that, for audio tokens to influence and activate concepts within text tokens, the LLM's attention mechanism, which facilitates inter-token interaction, is a \textit{necessary} condition. To investigate whether attention is also a \textit{sufficient} condition for this cross-modal concept activation, we introduce an architectural variant. 
In this variant, audio tokens interact with text tokens exclusively within the attention submodule of each LLM layer by passing the information from audio tokens to text tokens via causal attention. Subsequently, these audio representations are discarded and only the text tokens are propagated to the FFN submodules, as illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig_hyp1_2_3}(B). 
Regarding implementation, we project audio tokens separately as input for each LLM layer, pass them to the layer's attention mechanism, and then discard them, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig_hyp1_2_3}(B).  While specific implementation details and further optimizations are deferred to section~\ref{sec_hyp3_multi}, Appendix~\ref{apx_effi_connector} and Table~\ref{tab_effi_connector}, our primary objective here is to evaluate the hypothesis that processing audio information exclusively through the LLM's attention mechanism, followed by discarding it, is both a necessary and sufficient condition for effective audio-language integration. Empirical results, presented in Table~\ref{tab_variant_comparision}, indicate that this architectural modification maintains or improves performance across all three stages of our training curriculum (Section~\ref{exp_setup}) compared to the preceding variant.

\textbf{Leveraging parametric versus contextual knowledge}: Here we posit how this architectural modification utilizes two types of knowledge inherent in pre-trained LLMs: (1) parametric knowledge, primarily embedded within the FFN layers as a result of extensive language pre-training, and (2) contextual knowledge, which is dynamically incorporated through attention mechanisms. The empirical success of this variant shows that audio input, as contextual information, can effectively induce required concept activations in text token representations via attention-based modulation, without needing direct FFN processing of audio representations. Consequently, audio information indirectly accesses the LLM's parametric knowledge: the audio context "piggybacks" on text tokens, as attention mechanisms reconfigure these representations, which then engage relevant concept-related pathways during FFN processing. This outcome demonstrates that robust cross-modal concept alignment is attainable while preserving the integrity of the LLM's pre-trained linguistic knowledge, predominantly encoded in its FFNs. Such a strategy offers gains in architectural efficiency and provides deeper insights into multimodal information integration.

Integrating audio information exclusively via an LLM layer's attention submodule, without propagating it to the layer's FFN submodule, is sufficient for the LLM to effectively probe audio representations and engage relevant pathways during FFN processing to satisfy textual queries. This method maintains or improves performance and may preserve the FFN's pre-trained linguistic knowledge while still facilitating cross-modal information transfer.
\end{tcolorbox}

\subsection{Hypothesis 3: Encoder ensembles enhance audio-LLM performance} %% Exp 5 SSLAM+CLAP+MUSIC Encoders Exp 5 (AllmAttnOnlyVisSamMMProjLGapWithAudQMutiEnc)
\label{sec_hyp3_multi}
Audio representation learning research is notably specialized, encompassing distinct sub-disciplines for speech (e.g., Whisper~\cite{radford2023robust}, LAION-CLAP-Speech~\cite{wu2023large}), music (e.g., MERT~\cite{li2023mert}, LAION-CLAP-Music~\cite{wu2023large}), and general audio (e.g., SSLAM~\cite{alex2025sslam}, LAION-CLAP-General~\cite{wu2023large}). This divergence contrasts with modalities like vision, where general-purpose encoders such as DINOv2~\cite{oquab2024dinov2learningrobustvisual} can effectively represent a broad range of RGB images. Consequently, for audio-LLMs designed to handle diverse auditory inputs (spanning music, speech, and general audio), the use of specialized encoders, or ensembles thereof, becomes a critical consideration.

Furthermore, prior work on audio-LLMs (e.g., LTU~\cite{gong2024listen}, GAMA~\cite{ghosh2024gama}, Audio Flamingo~\cite{alayrac2022flamingo}) has demonstrated that employing language-aligned audio encoders significantly improves model performance. This enhancement is attributed to the initial alignment between audio representations and the language modality. Consequently, a common practice involves an additional phase of text-audio pre-training for audio encoders, which were originally trained via self-supervised or supervised methods (e.g., CAV-MAE~\cite{gong2022contrastive} in LTU, AST~\cite{gong2021ast} in GAMA), prior to their integration into the audio-LLM framework. However, this subsequent language alignment, while enhancing the integration with LLMs, may inadvertently diminish the rich, fine-grained representational capacity inherent in the original self-supervised pre-training. Studies such as Cambrian-1~\cite{tong2024cambrian} and LongVU~\cite{shen2024longvu} have explored this trade-off, suggesting that while language-aligned encoders excel at capturing dominant concepts, non-contrastive self-supervised learning objectives tend to preserve more detailed, fine-grained information.

To evaluate this hypothesis, we augmented the SSLAM encoder (audio encoder used in variants discussed in Section~\ref{sec_baseline_arch},~\ref{sec_hyp1_delay},~\ref{sec_hyp2_attn}) with additional audio encoders (Figure~\ref{fig_hyp1_2_3}(D)). Specifically, we incorporated LAION-CLAP-general~\cite{wu2023large}, LAION-CLAP-music and speech~\cite{wu2023large}. The latent token-based connector module enables us to integrate as many audio encoders as desired without increasing the LLM input tokens. These additional encoders are language-aligned, additionally pre-trained on extensive general audio, music, and speech datasets, respectively. The rationale for this ensemble is that the self-supervised SSLAM encoder provides rich, fine-grained semantic information. Concurrently, the CLAP encoders contribute robust, language-aligned representations specialized for their respective domains: general audio, music, and speech. This combination aims to equip the network with a more comprehensive and versatile understanding of diverse auditory inputs. The empirical results from our three-stage experimental setup (Section~\ref{exp_setup}) for this multi-encoder configuration are presented in Table~\ref{tab_variant_comparision}.
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=gray!10!white, colframe=gray!75!black, title=\textbf{Finding 3}]
Multi-audio encoder ensembles broaden an LLM's audio querying capabilities, enabling it to query a wide range of audio information. Employing a diverse ensemble of audio encoders, which combines self-supervised for fine-grained details, language-aligned for better language alignment, and domain-specific for areas like music and speech, provides richer, complementary representations. Notably, we demonstrate an efficient integration mechanism for such ensembles that avoids increasing the LLM's input token count, leading to improved overall performance.
\end{tcolorbox}
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%

\textbf{Connector module}: Our connector module consists of two main operations: cross-attention between latent tokens and audio encoder outputs, followed by projection of these latent tokens to the LLM's hidden dimension~\cite{tong2024cambrian, shen2024longvu}. The connector initializes with a single latent token that is replicated into $n$ tokens, where $n$ is determined by the resolution of the audio encoder output. These replicated latent tokens perform cross-attention with output representations from multiple audio encoders while preserving time and frequency resolution information. Specifically, each latent token interacts with a designated region across all output encoders to gather information from that region, as illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig_hyp1_2_3} (C). Following cross-attention, these information-enriched latent tokens are projected to match the LLM's hidden dimension. For experiments where audio information is integrated exclusively into the attention submodule of specific LLM layers (Sections~\ref{sec_hyp2_attn} and~\ref{sec_hyp3_multi}), we employ one connector to prepare audio inputs for each LLM layer where audio-LLM integration occurs. Our experiments demonstrate that this process can be further optimized with similar or improved performance by sharing the cross-attention modules across layers, which we discuss in detail in the supplementary material.

\section{Discussion: Performance relative to prior art}

While our primary contribution is a systematic investigation of audio-LLM architectural strategies and their impact on information transfer, we provide performance comparisons with prior systems in Table~\ref{tab_audio_llm_comparison} for context. To ensure fair comparison, we evaluated using identical stochastic decoding parameters (matching the top-$p$, top-$k$, and temperature values) as those employed in LTU's evaluation protocol.

Our final architecture, PAL (Probing Audio representation LLM), which incorporates all insights derived from Hypotheses 1-3, demonstrates competitive or superior performance across multiple benchmarks despite these computational disadvantages. This outcome highlights the significance of our architectural innovations, suggesting that optimized cross-modal information transfer can effectively compensate for reduced model scale and training resources.

\section{Experimental setup}
\label{exp_setup}
In this section, we define the standardized experimental setup used for our experiments. These components are used throughout this comparative study, ensuring fairness in the experiments. Additional training details are provided in Appendix~\ref{apx_hyperparams}.

\subsection{Training curriculum}
\label{training_curriculum}
We employ the three-stage pre-training and fine-tuning curriculum and data proposed by LTU~\cite{gong2024listen}.

\textbf{Stage 1: Connector pre-training.} We begin by pre-training the newly added connector modules (i.e., any new layers introduced to connect the audio encoder with the LLM). In this stage, we utilize approximately 1.2 M audio question-answer data points focused on classification and acoustic descriptions. The LLM parameters are kept frozen to prevent catastrophic forgetting. The use of deterministic question-answer pairs trains the connector module to extract relevant information from the audio encoder outputs required by the LLM, while simultaneously preventing the LLM from generating lengthy or hallucinated responses.

\textbf{Stage 2: Initial fine-tuning.} In this stage, all components, excluding the audio encoder, undergo fine-tuning. The training data is augmented with additional closed-ended question-answer pairs, bringing the total to 1.9 M such pairs.

\textbf{Stage 3: Final fine-tuning.} In the final stage, we continue to fine-tune all components except the audio encoder. We augment the dataset with open-ended question-answer pairs, bringing the total dataset size to approximately 5.6 M examples.



\subsection{Training data}
We utilize OpenAQA-5M, the audio question-answer (QA) pair dataset proposed by LTU~\cite{gong2024listen}. This dataset, comprising approximately 5.6 million (audio, question, answer) tuples in our downloaded version, is sourced from publicly-available audio datasets. The QA pairs include closed-ended questions for fundamental audio perception (e.g., classification, acoustic characteristics, temporal information) and open-ended questions, generated using GPT-3.5. Further details regarding the dataset composition and generation are provided in Appendix~\ref{apx_datasets}.

\subsection{Evaluation strategy: audio Encoder to LLM information transfer}

As previously described, our primary goal is to determine whether critical audio event information successfully transfers from the audio encoder to the LLM's latent representation space. We posit that the audio-LLM's performance on downstream classification tasks effectively indicates the quality of this information transfer. Following LTU's evaluation framework~\cite{gong2024listen}, we implement two complementary assessment methods: 1) for classification datasets, we measure semantic similarity by encoding both the model's text outputs and target audio event labels using gpt-text-embedding-ada; and 2) for captioning capabilities, we employ standard audio captioning datasets and evaluate generated descriptions using established metrics including CIDEr and SPICE.

To ensure reproducibility and determinism during inference, we employ greedy decoding. This deterministic approach selects the most probable token at each step, contrasting with stochastic sampling strategies (e.g., top-$k$ or top-$p$) utilized in the evaluation of previous works such as LTU and GAMA.


\subsection{LLM}
We used Llama-3.2 1B~\cite{grattafiori2024llama} for all experiments in the analysis of architectural design hypotheses (Section~\ref{arch_analysis}).

\section{Literature review}
\label{sec_lit_review_audio_llm_arch}

\textbf{Audio-LLM architectures}:
Architectures for audio-LLMs primarily diverge into two main paradigms for integrating audio information with pre-trained LLMs. The first, often referred to as the Pengi~\cite{deshmukh2023pengi} or LLaVA~\cite{liu2023visual} style, is adopted by models such as Pengi, LTU~\cite{gong2024listen}, SALMONN~\cite{tang2024salmonn}, and GAMA~\cite{ghosh2024gama}. In these systems, audio embeddings, derived from an audio encoder, are projected into the LLM's token embedding space. These audio tokens are then typically prepended to the text tokens and processed jointly through the LLM's layers. This approach treats audio information akin to additional text, subjecting it to both the attention and FFN submodules within each LLM layer. The implications and necessity of processing audio representations through FFNs, which are primarily trained for linguistic patterns, warrant further investigation.

An alternative approach is inspired by the Flamingo architecture~\cite{alayrac2022flamingo}, as seen in models like Audio-Flamingo~\cite{kong2024audio}. This paradigm introduces new, dedicated cross-modal layers, comprising cross-attention and FFN blocks, interleaved between the existing LLM layers. Within these inserted layers, text tokens from a given LLM layer \( l \) perform cross-attention to the audio tokens before the text representations proceed to the subsequent LLM layer \( l+1 \). While this allows for explicit and gated interaction with audio features, it necessitates the addition of new FFN and cross-attention modules, leading to a considerable increase in model parameters and computational overhead.

\textbf{Instruction tuning and reasoning capabilities in audio-LLMs}:
Beyond architectural design, a significant research thrust aims to enhance audio-LLM instruction-following and reasoning. This involves creating specialized datasets and benchmarks for rigorous evaluation. For instance, works like~\cite{sakshi2024mmau, deshmukh2025audio, deshmukh2025adiff} focus on evaluation metrics and datasets for audio reasoning, while~\cite{ghosh2024gama, ghosh2025audio} contribute high-quality instruction tuning datasets. Training existing audio-LLM architectures on these datasets scales their capabilities for complex reasoning and nuanced instruction adherence.

\section{Limitations and observations}
\label{sec_work_limitations}

Our work focuses on enhancing the LLM's ability to extract relevant information from audio representations to satisfy textual queries. Accordingly, our evaluation methodology primarily included audio event classification tasks to assess whether the LLM could accurately capture audio events and temporal information from audio representations. Additionally, we incorporated audio captioning tasks to evaluate descriptive capabilities.

While our evaluations did not extend to complex reasoning abilities or other advanced tasks that typically require substantial, specialized instruction tuning, we supplemented our quantitative benchmarks with a qualitative analysis comparing our approach to previous works. This analysis provides additional insight, suggesting that our model achieves comparable or superior quality scores on the examined samples. Sample outputs with corresponding qualitative evaluations are presented in Appendix~\ref{apx_sample_output}. These encouraging results highlight the potential for targeted instruction tuning to achieve further substantial gains when leveraging our foundational improvements to audio-text information transfer. 


\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec_conclusion}

In this work, we conducted a systematic investigation into the architectural mechanisms governing efficient information transfer from audio encoders to LLMs, conceptualizing effective interaction as the LLM's ability to proficiently probe audio representations. Guided by hypotheses derived from mechanistic interpretability and LLM operational principles, we systematically evaluated several novel audio-LLM integration strategies.

Our findings validate three key architectural insights: (1) delaying audio integration allows LLMs to first establish crucial textual context, enhancing their ability to query audio information effectively; (2) processing audio representations exclusively through the LLM's attention submodules, without propagation to FFNs, is a sufficient and efficient mechanism for cross-modal concept activation; and (3) employing a diverse ensemble of audio encoders significantly broadens the LLM's capacity to probe a wider variety of audio information. These insights were consistently supported by empirical evidence from a rigorous three-stage training curriculum on a publicly-available dataset, ensuring fair and controlled comparisons.

The culmination of these findings is a novel audio-LLM architecture (PAL) that, by incorporating these principled design choices, demonstrates substantial relative performance improvements ranging from 10\% to 60\% over a standard baseline. This study not only provides actionable architectural recommendations for building more effective audio-LLMs but also contributes to a deeper understanding of how to optimize cross-modal information flow in such systems. The insights gained here lay a strong foundation for future work aimed at developing audio-LLMs with even more advanced capabilities in understanding complex acoustic environments and engaging in sophisticated audio-grounded reasoning.

\section{Datasets}
\label{apx_datasets}

We follow the training data(OpenAQA) and evaluation data proposed by LTU~\cite{gong2024listen}. This section gives information about the different datasets used in training and evaluation sets.

\subsection{Training datasets}

\textbf{AudioSet-2M} ~\cite{gemmeke2017audio}: 
Audioset-2M is a large-scale multi-label dataset containing 2 million 10-second audio clips from Youtube videos. Each clip has one or more audio event labels annotated at the clip level without temporal boundaries (onset/offset information), making them weakly labeled. OpenAQA utilizes a 500K sample subset to maintain audio source diversity and prevent single-source dominance.

\textbf{Temporally-strongly label AudioSet}~\cite{hershey2021benefit}: An improved AudioSet subset with temporal boundaries. Contains 934,821 sound events across 103,463 10-second clips, with onset/offset annotations. The modified label set includes 447 classes (376 derived from the original 528). OpenAQA utilizes all 101,791 training samples, with 91,075 enhanced by WavCaps captions~\cite{mei2023wavcaps}.

\textbf{VGGSound}~\cite{chen2020vggsound}: VGGSound dataset is the collection of audio data collected from Youtube containing 200K samples of 10-second audio clips with 309 classes annotated to each sample. OpenAQA uses only 183,727 samples for training.

\textbf{FreeSound}~\cite{font2013freesound}: Freesound is an online collaborative sound sharing platform established in 2005, hosting over 560K audio clips. OpenAQA ~\cite{gong2024listen} uses 91,434 audio clips, each less than 10 seconds in duration captioned by WavCaps ~\cite{mei2023wavcaps} for training.

\textbf{FSD50K}~\cite{fonseca2021fsd50k}: FSD50K contains the audio clips collected from the Freesound dataset, consisting of 200 sound class annotations based on the AudioSet ontology. The training and validation sets contain 37,134 and 4,170, respectively. OpenAQA uses 41,304 audio samples from both training and validation sets for training. 

\textbf{AudioCaps}~\cite{kim2019audiocaps}: AudioCaps is an audio captioning dataset constructed from a subset of AudioSet with enhanced human annotation of audio captions collected from Amazon Mechanical Turk. The training and validation sets originally consist of 49,838 and 495 audio clips, respectively. For the training set, each audio clip is paired with a single caption, while in the validation set, each audio clip is paired with five captions. OpenAQA uses both training and validation sets but only used 46,462 audio clips and 48,298 captions.

\textbf{Clotho V2}~\cite{drossos2020clotho}: Clotho is an audio captioning dataset comprising audio clips sourced from Freesound, with captions collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk. Each audio clip is paired with five captions. OpenAQA uses 3,741 clips from the development set and 1,045 clips from the validation set for training.


\textbf{Sound-Bible}~\cite{soundbible}: Sound-Bible is an online platform that provides sound effects and audio clips. OpenAQA uses 1,225 audio clips from this source, each captioned by the WavCaps project~\cite{mei2023wavcaps}.

\subsection{Evaluation Datasets}

% We utilized datasets such as VocalSound, ESC-50...... Below, we provide additional details about datasets not previously discussed.


\textbf{VocalSound}~\cite{gong2022vocalsound}: The VocalSound dataset consists of 21,024 crowd-sourced recordings of 6 different classes of vocal expressions collected from 3,365 unique subjects. We evaluated our model on the VocalSound evaluation set which contains 3,594 audio clips, and report top-1 accuracy scores across the 6 classes for single-class classification performance. It is important to note that VocalSound was excluded from our training data; therefore, our evaluation on VocalSound is considered zero-shot.

\textbf{ESC-50}~\cite{piczak2015esc}: The ESC-50 dataset comprises 2,000 five-second environmental audio clips categorized into 50 different classes. Following~\cite{gong2024listen}, we evaluate our model on all 2,000 audio samples and report the top-1 accuracy score for single-class classification performance. It is important to note that while ESC-50 is originally sampled from the Freesound dataset (which is included in our training data), ESC-50 itself was excluded from training. Therefore, our evaluation on this dataset is considered a weak zero-shot evaluation.

\textbf{DCASE2017 task 4} (DCASE)~\cite{Mesaros2019_TASLP}: DCASE 2017 Task 4 contains 17 sound events distributed across two categories: "Warning" and "Vehicle". The evaluation set consists of 1,350 audio clips. We evaluated our model on this dataset and report micro F1-score(MiF1) for single-class classification performance. It is important to note that DCASE 2017 task 4 is originally sampled from AudioSet, which is included in our training data. However, DCASE 2017 task 4 itself is excluded from training, making our evaluation on this dataset a weak zero-shot evaluation.

\textbf{FSD50K} (FSD) \cite{fonseca2021fsd50k}: The FSD50K evaluation set contains 10,231 audio clips. We evaluated our model on this evaluation set and report the mAP score for multi-label classification performance. Since the training and validation sets of FSD50K are included in our training data, this evaluation is considered an in-domain evaluation.

\textbf{AudioSet}~\cite{gemmeke2017audio}: We evaluated our model on this evaluation set and report the mAP score for multi-label classification performance. The training set of AudioSet is included in our training data, making this evaluation an in-domain evaluation.

\textbf{AudioCaps}~\cite{kim2019audiocaps}: The AudioCaps evaluation set contains 901 audio clips, each paired with 5 audio captions, resulting in a total of 4,505 audio-caption pairs. We evaluated our model on this evaluation set and report the captioning scores using CIDER and SPICE metrics. The training and validation sets of AudioCaps are included in our training data, making this evaluation an in-domain evaluation.

\textbf{Clotho V2}~\cite{drossos2020clotho}: The Clotho V2 evaluation set contains 1,045 audio clips, each paired with 5 audio captions, resulting in a total of 5,225 audio-caption pairs. We evaluated our model on this evaluation set and report the captioning scores using CIDER and SPICE metrics. The development and validation sets of Clotho V2 are included in our training data, making this evaluation an in-domain evaluation.

\section{Efficient implementation of connector modules in Hypothesis 2}
\label{apx_effi_connector}

Our connector module consists of two primary submodules: (1) a latent-to-audio cross-attention module that enables latent tokens to attend to audio token representations, and (2) a projection module that maps these attended latent representations from their lower dimension to the LLM's hidden dimension before passing them to the corresponding LLM layer.

For Hypothesis 2, we explored two architectural variants to connect audio representations with the LLM. The first variant used independent connectors for each LLM layer, requiring audio integration. Each connector contained its own latent token (initially a single token per layer, later replicated to match the resolution of the audio encoder output), cross-attention module, and projection layer. In the second variant, we implemented a more parameter-efficient approach by sharing a single cross-attention module and latent token across all LLM layers, while maintaining layer-specific projection modules to accommodate different hidden dimensions.

Our experimental results revealed that both architectural variants (shared and separate connectors) achieved comparable performance (Table~\ref{tab_effi_connector}) despite their difference in parameter count. These findings indicate that the specific implementation of connectors, whether shared across layers or implemented separately, has minimal impact on model effectiveness once a fundamental cross-modal connection mechanism is established. This suggests that, after ensuring proper information flow between modalities, additional efficiency optimizations can be implemented without compromising performance.

\section{Ethical considerations and societal impact}
\label{apx_ethics_and_impact}

\subsection{Broader impacts}

\textbf{Potential positive societal impacts:}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Accessibility}: Enhanced audio understanding for assistive technologies and hearing aids
    \item \textbf{Audio Content Understanding}: Improved capabilities for searching, indexing, and analyzing audio archives
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Potential negative societal impacts and mitigation:}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Security concerns}: While not specialized for speech recognition in regards to training data, improved audio understanding could be repurposed for surveillance applications
    \item \textbf{Bias and fairness}: Audio-LLMs may perform unequally across different accents, dialects, or acoustic conditions
    \item \textbf{Reliability issues}: In critical applications, incorrect audio understanding could have serious consequences
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Mitigation strategy}: We advocate for responsible application with appropriate oversight, diverse evaluation datasets, and human-in-the-loop approaches for critical use cases.

\subsection{Safeguards}

As our work focuses on architectural research, we implement the following safeguards:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Data policy}: We exclusively use publicly available audio data, no private audio recordings.
    \item \textbf{Research transparency}: We provide detailed documentation of architectural choices and evaluation methods.
    \item \textbf{Model release}: We plan to release our model weights upon acceptance with appropriate safeguards, including clear usage guidelines prohibiting malicious applications to promote responsible use.
\end{itemize}

title: EuroCrops: All you need to know about the Largest Harmonised Open Crop Dataset Across the European Union
summary:
EuroCrops contains geo-referenced polygons of agricultural croplands from 16
countries of the European Union (EU) as well as information on the respective
crop species grown there. These semantic annotations are derived from
self-declarations by farmers receiving subsidies under the Common Agriculture
Policy (CAP) of the European Commission (EC). Over the last 1.5 years, the
individual national crop datasets have been manually collected, the crop
classes have been translated into the English language and transferred into the
newly developed Hierarchical Crop and Agriculture Taxonomy (HCAT). EuroCrops is
publicly available under continuous improvement through an active user
community.

\begin{abstract}
  EuroCrops contains geo-referenced polygons of agricultural croplands from 16 countries of the \gls{gl:eu} as well as information on the respective crop species grown there.   
  These semantic annotations are derived from self-declarations by farmers receiving subsidies under the \gls{gl:cap} of the \gls{gl:ec}.  
  Over the last 1.5 years, the individual national crop datasets have been manually collected, the crop classes have been translated into the English language and transferred into the newly developed \gls{gl:hcat}. 
  
  EuroCrops is publicly available under continuous improvement through an active user community.
  
  \glsresetall
\end{abstract}

\section{Background \& Summary}

As\blfootnote{Preprint. Under review.} the world's population continues to grow and global climate change becomes increasingly apparent, enhancing the efficiency and resilience of agriculture at both the local and global level is a crucial challenge for humanity's future.
Recent developments in satellite-based \gls{gl:eo} have provided us with the ability to observe and analyse the processes occurring on the Earth's surface in near real-time.
By leveraging machine learning and artificial intelligence, we can extract valuable insights from these enormous volumes of high-quality and information-rich data, which can inform the development of functional process models for the monitoring of agricultural crops and the design of future applications.
For example, the activity of these vegetation stands could be monitored and deviations from the expected progression, and thus the expected crop yields, could be detected.
Based on this information, farmers would be able to initiate countermeasures at an early stage.
This would make a decisive contribution to food security, representing one of the central \glspl{gl:sdg} stated by the \gls{gl:un}.
However, these possibilities are massively limited by the insufficient availability of qualitative reference data, which are necessary for the creation of functional process models on the basis of such Earth observation data.

The EuroCrops project aims to show how this gap can be filled by compiling administrative data assessed in the context of agricultural subsidy control in the \gls{gl:eu} area, exemplified by a first pilot project.\cite{schneider2021epe}
In light of previous studies, e.g., BreizhCrops \cite{russwurm2020breizhcrops}, ZueriCrop \cite{turkoglu2021crop}, and CropHarvest \cite{tseng2021cropharvest}, the key objectives of EuroCrops lie in the extension of both the variability of crop species classes to be represented and the geographical scale of the considered regions.

For this purpose, we collected geo-referenced crop datasets from three countries within Europe, harmonised the data by translating the crop names and developed an hierarchical structure to order the occurring crops.
Finally, the crop labels were paired with the corresponding Sentinel-2 \gls{gl:eo} data and we released the TinyEuroCrops\cite{schneider2021tinyeurocrops} dataset publicly via the repository of the Technical University of Munich.
Despite faced with some challenges, we soon realised that the dataset gained its popularity not due to the satellite data, but due to the fact that we also published the geo-referenced field polygon vector data together with the harmonised information of which crop species were cultivated there for a certain year.
Having this data prepared in one reconciled format, language, and centrally available across borders and not just on a national level sparked the discussions about its broad applicability in various domains.
The fact that this data has been prepared in a joint standardised format and language and that it is centrally available across borders and not only at national level has triggered discussion about its broad applicability in various areas.
The research questions related to the analysis of agricultural diversity and food security in Europe were one of the reasons for the popularity of the dataset, leading to the motivation to extend them spatially and later also temporally.

In this article, we present and describe the first spatially extended EuroCrops vector dataset.
For this release, we manually collected the raw crop declaration data from 16 \gls{gl:eu} countries, which was made available and distributed across multiple platforms and servers.
After translating the textual declarations data, we developed a new version of our \gls{gl:hcat}\cite{schneider2021epe} in order to organize all crops that are cultivated within the \gls{gl:eu} into a common hierarchical representation scheme.
The process of this development is visualised in Figure \ref{fig:process} and will be further explained in the methods section.

By being able to analyse agricultural data at this expanded spatial scale, which extends from Sweden to Portugal, we hope to enable researchers to carry out their work across borders and gain new insights.
We further publish the sources and links to the original datasets\cite{schneider2022githubwiki} and provide mappings\cite{schneider2022githubmappings} from the national crop class representation into \gls{gl:hcat} on our GitHub\cite{schneider2022github} repository.
This way, it is now possible to extend the dataset in time to the desired year by linking the mapping to a national dataset that can be found on the respective websites.

\section*{Methods}
\label{sec:methods}

In order to compile the presented dataset, several iterative steps had to be performed, which can roughly be grouped into \textit{data collection}, \textit{harmonisation} and  \textit{validation}, denoted as \textbf{A}, \textbf{B} and \textbf{C} in Figure \ref{fig:process} and will be further described in the next subsections.
Data obtained from each member state of the \gls{gl:eu} has to undergo the entire procedure, sometimes even multiple times, as indicated by the stacked layers in Figure \ref{fig:process} and arrows going from each countries \texttt{Update HCAT} process back to the beginning and the \texttt{Automatic mapping to HCAT} for the individual dataset.
This recurring loop is the main reason for the exponentially increasing amount of manual work that was necessary for the creation of the dataset and required careful deliberation on the right moment for cutting the development of \gls{gl:hcat}.


\subsection*{A. Data Collection}

As EuroCrops consists of multiple smaller datasets, the data collection itself plays an integral role.
This paper will focus on the practical part of that process, whereas an in-depth analysis of the challenges of creating a transnational dataset is described in more detail by Schneider et al. \cite{schneider2022challenges}.\\
Generally, we identified four ways of data acquisition:
Firstly, many countries publish national crop data on the webpage of the respective ministry or agency responsible for agricultural, food or rural topics.
Some countries instead offer a national geoportal, distributing different kinds of geodata specifically or, as another mean of distribution, publishing geodata on an international level, e.g. via \texttt{INSPIRE}\cite{inspire2022inspire} or \texttt{data.europe.eu}\cite{commission2022data}.
Lastly, if the data is not openly distributed on a webpage or geoportal, we reached out personally to ministries or agencies and asked for the data directly.
Most of the national datasets used in the EuroCrops project were collected from national ministry webpages or geoportals as listed in Tables \ref{tab:ministries} and \ref{tab:geoportal} respectively, mostly made available as \emph{ESRI shapefiles}, \texttt{GeoJSON}, or \texttt{GeoPackage} \texttt{(GPKG)}.
Nonetheless, some data can only be accessed via a \gls{gl:wfs} implemented in a \gls{gl:gis}, allowing the user to display the desired data and save it in a chosen file format.
The other means of data access are shown in Tables \ref{tab:direct} and \ref{tab:international}.
Figure \ref{fig:diagrams} puts all this information into context, gives an overview of the available datasets, and indicates from where the data originates.
Countries marked yellow in Figure \ref{fig:diagrams} indicate only partial availability of crop data for the respective country.
%For some countries, it was not possible to obtain data from the entire country which is indicated in yellow in Figure \ref{fig:diagrams}.\\
In order to give a better understanding of the original raw datasets we got from the countries, we visualised a small fraction of the data from North-Rhine Westphalia (Germany) in Figure \ref{fig:nrw} with coloured geo-referenced agricultural parcel polygons.
Table \ref{tab:raw_data} gives an impression of how the corresponding original raw attribute table looks like.
Each row entry describes the crop species that has been cultivated on the associated parcel.

\subsection*{B. Harmonising Country-Specific Crop Classes}

After collecting the data and extracting the set of country-specific crop classes from the attribute tables, we initiated the harmonisation process.
This step is necessary because the crop names from each country usually come in the national language of the member states and without standardised codes, as shown in Table \ref{fig:nrw}.\\
Instead of working with the entire attribute table, we worked with a table showing the name and code of a certain crop class per row together with its absolute and relative occurrence in the dataset.
In Figure \ref{fig:process}, that file, preserving original crop class name and code, is denoted as \texttt{country\_year\_crops.csv}.\\
Following this, the \texttt{automatic translation} starts the process of harmonising the given original crop class names into the \gls{gl:hcat} taxonomy.
Therefore, multiple steps had to be performed:
The file \texttt{country\_year\_translated.csv} arises from the translation of the crop classes into English.
Despite the access to modern translation programmes, we were not able to automate this part end-to-end, as country-specific agricultural terms seem to cause mistranslations across all common translators.
By correcting the translations manually, we hope to bridge that gap and make the dataset as reliable as possible.
Similarly, mapping the translations to \gls{gl:hcat} was only possible to perform automatically to a certain degree and required \texttt{manual checks} (see Figure \ref{fig:process}) as well.
This was again caused by the diversity of the crop classes declared by the member states.\\
Within this process of manual translation and matching, we were able to catch most of the missing classes in our growing taxonomy.
The iterative \texttt{updates of HCAT} helped in the detailed classification of delivered datafiles by the countries, but also shed light on relevant and focus areas within the taxonomy.
% Kurze Beschreibung der aktuellen Struktur
To the matching \gls{gl:hcat} name, we also added the corresponding \gls{gl:hcat} code, which embeds the hierarchy of the taxonomy.
This way, we enriched the country-specific original crop name and code with our \gls{gl:hcat} name and code and the absolute and relative occurrence in a country.\\
Hence, we are able to visualise the number of instances of certain crop classes and compare the occurrences with those from other countries for general diversity analysis and taxonomy class updates.
% Kleine Überleitung
The preliminary file is stored in a \texttt{country\_year.csv} after positive assessment during working step \textbf{C}.

\subsection*{C. Community Work: Content Validation and Feedback Incorporation}

The largest expertise on country-specific crop classes still lies with the respective countries, driving to the decision to keep them onboard during the validation phase of the project.
Therefore, we asked all countries during the end phase of our pipeline if our translations and mappings seemed reasonable.
Out of 16 countries, we received feedback from seven who double-checked and reviewed our work.
While this increased the quality of the dataset, it also started another loop in the harmonisation block, which is visualised in Figure \ref{fig:process} as the arrow going from \texttt{Everything correct?} to \texttt{Manual verification}.
Eventually, we uploaded the first version of the dataset on our university-owned data-sharing platform and set up a GitHub repository\cite{schneider2022github} for the community to have a first look.
This resulted into several opened issues and pull requests where improvements to the mappings were suggested.
Each time we were content with a version of the mapping, we manually joined the original dataset with our mapping and saved it as a shapefile.
This lead to one shapefile for each country and five successive versions of the dataset incorporating the proposed changes from GitHub.
One exemplary attribute table of such a shapefile is shown in Table \ref{tab:ec_data}.
All of the versions were individually uploaded to Zenodo\cite{schneider2022ecz}, which now officially tracks the versions with a \gls{gl:doi}.

\section*{Data Records}

In the following paragraphs, all individual data sources are presented.
For each contributing country the data source, available years, coverage, licence, and format are described and referenced.
By doing so, we aspire to give the research community a tool to discover and access raw data faster and more reliably.

\paragraph{Austria}
The dataset for Austria comprises a vast range of years, spanning from 2015 to 2021.
Moreover, the whole territory of the country is covered without any regional omissions.
Crop classes are defined very detailed with an approximate number of 200 classes.
The files were made available in \texttt{GPKG} format via two platforms, the European “data.europa.eu”\cite{at2021data} and "data.gv.at"\cite{at2021data2}, a platform that distributes data of the public sector in Austria for further analysis and development.
However, both platforms receive the datasets from “Agrarmarkt Austria”, which is a public geodata office.
As such, data is published free of charge under the Creative Commons Licence CC-BY-AT 4.0.
In the course of the EuroCrops project, the dataset of 2021 was harmonised for Austria.

\paragraph{Belgium} %% TODO Wallonia Link
Due to the federal structure of Belgium, the data is split into two sets covering the regions of Flanders and Wallonia.
Not only is the data published via different platforms, its structure also differs heavily between the two regions.\\
The data for Flanders\cite{befl2021data} is published by the Department of Agriculture and Fishery on its website as shapefiles.
Additionally, a word document explaining the current state of the data as well as the abbreviations that occur in the attribute table of the shapefiles is available in Flemish language.
The crop classes are differentiated very precisely with an approximate number of 275 classes.
Datasets are available for the years 2019, 2020 and 2021.\\
The datasets for Wallonia are published by the Geoportal of Wallonia\cite{bew2016data} as shapefiles.
With an approximate number of 150 classes the crop classification of Wallonia is still quite precise, even though the Flemish data is more detailed.
On the other hand, a wider time period is captured by the Wallonian datasets, covering all years since 2015.\\
So far only the Flemish data for the year 2021 got harmonised in the course of the EuroCrops-Project.

\paragraph{Croatia}
The Croatian data \cite{hr2020data} is distributed in \texttt{GPKG} format via a platform managed by the Agency for Payments in Agriculture, Fisheries and Rural Development, where an abundant sequence of years is available ranging from 2011 to 2021.
Due to translation difficulties, we obtained the data directly from the Paying Agency, and while all regions of the country are covered by the dataset, its differentiation between 14 crop classes turns out to be rather coarse.
For EuroCrops, the data of 2020 was harmonised.

\paragraph{Denmark}
The dataset of Denmark \cite{dk2019data} comprises of only the mainland.
The Faroe Islands and Greenland are not included.
However, with an approximate number of 300 classes, the Danish crop taxonomy is very detailed.
Datasets are available since the year 2017.
The data is available as shapefiles provided by the Danish Agricultural Agency.
All the data provided is considered open data, which means it can be openly used and distributed.
The Danish data of 2019 was harmonised throughout the course of the EuroCrops Project.

\paragraph{Estonia}
The Estonian dataset \cite{ee2021data} is made available under the creative commons licence.
Thus, there are no limitations to public access.
It can be acquired via the INSPIRE Geoportal as \gls{gl:wfs}.
When accessing the data via a \gls{gl:wfs} URL in a \gls{gl:gis}, the dataset can be transformed and saved as \texttt{GeoJSON} for example.
It covers all of Estonia but only for the current year.
Thus, data from 2021 was harmonised.
However, the crop differentiation is very precise, leading to a high number of ca. 150 classes.

\paragraph{Finland}
The Finnish dataset \cite{fi2021data} covers all provinces of the country.
Data is available for the years 2020 and 2021.
However, none of the years got harmonised yet, as Finland provided its datasets very late after the harmonisation process was already completed.
The data differentiates between 200 classes roughly, which enables a very precise crop classification.
The Finish Food Authority distributes the data via a \gls{gl:wfs} under the Creative Commons Licence BY 4.0.
Consequently, the datasets were implemented into a \gls{gl:gis} and saved as shapefile.

\paragraph{France}
France publishes national geodata as open licence on the "data.gouv.fr" platform\cite{fr2018data_official} as \texttt{GPKG}- and shapefiles.
While the central point of distribution makes it easy to discover and access the data, the fact that each region has its own sub-dataset makes the platform barely usable for someone who needs the entirety of the French data.
Luckily, there is a second (unofficial) server\cite{fr2018data_cq} that hosts a combination of all these national datasets in shapefile format.
Additionally, an excel sheet is available, containing the descriptions of all crop abbreviations used in the datasets.
The class differentiation is moderate.
Approximately 70 crop classes are distinguished.
In the course of the project, datasets were downloaded for the years spanning from 2016 to 2019, of which the file for 2018 was harmonised.
The data covers not only the French mainland but also overseas territories.

\paragraph{Germany}
Due to the federal structure of Germany datasets are not published on a national level, but by each federal state ("Bundesland") individually.
Two datasets were acquired:
One covers Lower Saxony \cite{dels2021data} and another one North Rhine-Westphalia \cite{denrw2021data}.
Both datasets depict the crop situation of 2021 and have a very high class precision, distinguishing between ca. 240 crop classes. Both files are distributed as shapefiles, one on the online platform for Rural Development and Agricultural Promotion of Lower Saxony, the other one on the geoportal of North Rhine-Westphalia.
Both datasets are published under “data licence Germany - attribution - Version 2.0”.
For the sake of completeness, it is worth noting that Brandenburg also published its data\cite{debb2021data}, but has not been included into EuroCrops yet.

\paragraph{Latvia}
The Rural Support Service of Latvia provides a \gls{gl:wfs}, which can be used to implement and convert the Latvian files to \texttt{GeoJSON} or shapefile in a \gls{gl:gis}.
The data \cite{lv2021data} is open so there are no publishing restrictions.
The files cover the whole territory of the country and are available for 2021 and 2022.
The file for 2021 got harmonised in the course of the EuroCrops Project.
The class precision is very high, differentiating between 150 crop types approximately.

\paragraph{Lithuania}
The crop parcels of Lithuania \cite{lt2021data} are available as shapefiles for the year 2021 covering the whole territory of the country.
Consequently, data got harmonised for the aforementioned year.
The file differentiates between 24 crop classes only.
However, the chosen classes are precise.
Datasets of a similar low number of classes normally assign very general crop terms to the classes (i.e. vineyard, citrus fruits, grassland).
In the case of Lithuania, the crop types assigned to the classes are very specific.
Thus, the class precision can be defined as medium, despite its low number of actual classes.
The data is published via Geoportal.lt, a platform distributing Lithuanian geo-data as part of the INSPIRE directive.

\paragraph{Netherlands}
The Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate distributes datasets via a \gls{gl:wfs} on the platform PDOK \cite{nl2021data}.
The files comprise only the mainland of the Netherlands; overseas territories are not included.
The class precision is very high, encompassing around 320 different plant categories.
So far data is only available for the years 2020 and 2021, of which the file for 2020 was harmonised for EuroCrops.
The datasets fall under the CC0 1.0 licence category which does not impose any limitations to public access.

\paragraph{Portugal}
The Portuguese datasets \cite{pt2021data} are available since 2017, with the file for 2021 harmonised.
Data since 2020 covers the complete national territory of Portugal.
Contrarily, the files for 2017, 2018 and 2019 are split up into regional territories, which had to be merged in a first step.
Moreover, some of the Portuguese regions are missing whereas the national datasets provide a complete and uniform depiction of Portuguese crop cover.
Furthermore, the class precision differs between the regional and the national datasets.
The crop differentiation is moderate for the regional sets with ca. 50 to 150 classes, whereas it is more precise for the national datasets with more than 200 classes.
The files can be accessed via a \gls{gl:wfs} provided by the Portuguese Finance Institute of Agriculture and Fisheries.

\paragraph{Romania} Romania officially does not yet publish crop data but is, according to the \gls{gl:apia}, actively working towards it.
We therefore decided to add a coarse and only regional land cover dataset\cite{ro20xxdata} into EuroCrops in order to give an incentive and an idea of how Romanian data would be integrated in the future.

\paragraph{Slovenia}
The Slovenian dataset \cite{si2021data} covers the territory of the whole country and the years 2019, 2020 and 2021.
The file for 2021 got harmonised.
The class precision is high, with approximately 150 different crop classes.
The files are distributed as shapefiles at the website of the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Food.
Additionally, two text files are published which describe the crop codes assigned to the plants with one file being in Slovenian language, the other one in English.
All data is made publicly available without use restrictions, however, citing the source is required.

\paragraph{Slovakia}
Slovakian data \cite{sk2021data} is available for the years 2020, 2021 and 2022.
The datasets cover all regions of the country.
The file depicting the crop situation in 2021 was harmonised.
The class precision is very high, differentiating between roughly 170 crop types.
The data was sent directly to the project members via e-mail by the Slovakian Agricultural Paying Agency.

\paragraph{Spain}
Spain distributes data under the licence CC BY 4.0 separately for each of its autonomous communities where each one has their own website.
The crop parcel data can be downloaded there as a shapefile in most cases.
So far data has been acquired for the communities of Castile and León, Andalusia and Navarra for the years 2020 and 2021. The Navarra dataset \cite{esna2021data} for 2021 got harmonised.
However, the data is very coarse, differentiating between 21 classes only.

\paragraph{Sweden}
\texttt{GeoJSON} files covering the crop parcels of all of Sweden for the years 2020 and 2021 were sent by a contact person at the Swedish Board of Agriculture\cite{se2021data} to the project members by email.
The files have a medium class precision distinguishing between ca. 80 classes, are published under the CC BY 4.0 licence and data depicting the crop situation in 2021 got harmonised.

\section*{Technical Validation}

Regarding the correctness of the underlying original data, it is important to stress that self-declarations build the basis of the input.
From official site, the in-situ controls act as a validation instance to these declarations, but these are just sparse samples and would never be able to cover the entire area.
One approach to actually validate the original data on a bigger scale was introduced by Gounari et al. \cite{gounari2022filtering}, but this would exceed the project tasks.
On our side, we concentrated on a valid harmonisation of the entire dataset.
The validation of the content itself was already discussed in the methods section.\\
In addition to our own approach, the \gls{gl:jrc} of the European Commission is  running validation experiments\cite{schneider2022githubissue7} with their \gls{gl:jrc} MARS database where they compare the areas of the official Eurostats declarations with the ones in EuroCrops.
This is still an ongoing effort and any findings of that will be published together with further EuroCrops versions.

\section*{Usage Notes}

The data is currently published as one shapefile per country on Zenodo\cite{schneider2022ecz} which can, for instance, be opened with \textsc{QGIS}\cite{qgis0000qgis}.
The corresponding mapping\cite{schneider2022githubmappings} files on GitHub are in CSV format with the structure found in Table \ref{tab:mapping}.
In order to use data from a year that has not been harmonised within EuroCrops, it is possible to join the mapping file of a country with the raw vector data file which can be found on the provided national platforms.
By using the correct column in the original dataset, which is indicated in the wiki\cite{schneider2022githubwiki} entry under "Attribute Table" for each country, also other datasets can be harmonised.
This might lead to some missing crop types, as our taxonomy only holds the crop classes occluding in the stated sub-datasets, but we assume that the majority of the crops should be covered.

title: Learning from Uncertain Data: From Possible Worlds to Possible Models
summary:
We introduce an efficient method for learning linear models from uncertain
data, where uncertainty is represented as a set of possible variations in the
data, leading to predictive multiplicity. Our approach leverages abstract
interpretation and zonotopes, a type of convex polytope, to compactly represent
these dataset variations, enabling the symbolic execution of gradient descent
on all possible worlds simultaneously. We develop techniques to ensure that
this process converges to a fixed point and derive closed-form solutions for
this fixed point. Our method provides sound over-approximations of all possible
optimal models and viable prediction ranges. We demonstrate the effectiveness
of our approach through theoretical and empirical analysis, highlighting its
potential to reason about model and prediction uncertainty due to data quality
issues in training data.

title: Open Sky, Open Threats: Replay Attacks in Space Launch and Re-entry Phases
summary:
This paper examines the effects of replay attacks on the integrity of both
uplink and downlink communications during critical phases of spacecraft
communication. By combining software-defined radios (SDRs) with a real-time
channel emulator, we replicate realistic attack conditions on the Orion
spacecraft's communication systems in both launch and reentry. Our evaluation
shows that, under replay attacks, the attacker's signal can overpower
legitimate transmissions, leading to a Signal to Noise Ratio (SNR) difference
of up to -7.8 dB during reentry and -6.5 dB during launch. To mitigate these
threats, we propose a more secure receiver design incorporating a
phase-coherency-dependent decision-directed (DD) equalizer with a narrowed
phase-locked loop (PLL) bandwidth. This configuration enhances resilience by
making synchronization more sensitive to phase distortions caused by replay
interference.
